text:
To His Excellency
President Lincoln
The undersigned Citizens of the State of
New York, respectfully ask the promotion of
Lieut. Col. Oliver S. Shepherd of the U.S.A.
to the office of Inspector General.
Col. Shepherd is a native of this State
and since the year 1840 has been engaged in
most of the Battles fought under our glorious
flag from Florida to Mexico.
Whenever present, he has won glory
for our cause, and been frequently breveted for
gallant conduct.
Where nearly all others proved treacherous
he brought safely from Texas, the last Regiment
of Regulars, which left that state after the
treason of Twiggs.
His regiment of regulars was the first
to pass through Baltimore after the 19th of April
1861.
He is now in Kentucky at the head of
his Regiment under General Thomas, but in
these times, when he has so few, if any, superiors
in the Army, we do cheerfully reccommend him
for a position of more extended usefulness.
Dated February 22, 1862
Hugh White
Jno. Cramus
Jno. Stuart

text: Alton, Ills., March 13th 1862 Dear Sir: Being at leisure and looking for some old papers I came to the enclosed document, being, as I Judge from the handwriting the original instructions given by Mr. Lincoln to Dr. Merryman in the affair between himself and Gen. Shields in 1842. I think it is the original document from the fact of it being in Mr. Lincoln's hand, and also from the interlineations and erasures. His willingness to do all that could be reasonably required of him in order to avoid the difficulty, and yet his quiet and dignified determination to submit to no wrong in the settlement of the same, so accords with the course pursued by him and his administration during the year he has been at the head of affairs in our government, that his course in each case will well bear comparison, and shows that the Mr. Lincoln of '42 was endowed with the same firmness and decision which has since been displayed by President Lincoln during the past year. If you please will you show it to him at your convenience; it may provoke a smile or perhaps a relation of the events to which it relates. We all feel encouraged now, since he has assumed the control of our army. The people have confidence in him, and will sustain him in such a manner that no “lost townships” will have to be looked up at the close of the rebellion. The Springfield folks are quite healthy, and the home guards have quite frequent glympses of Secesh uniforms in the neighborhood. W. H. Bailhache now has charge of the Qmasters department in Springfield. After the order for the reorganization of the 1st Cavalry, Col. Marshall, I received my
title: Abraham Lincoln papers: Series 1. General Correspondence. 1833-1916: Thomas S. Pinckard to John G. Nicolay, Thursday, March 13, 1862 (Sends documents pertaining to the duel between Lincoln and Shields)

text: commission as First Lieutenant, but owing to the ill health of my family as well as my own ill health I was compelled to resign, which I did the first of this month. I am troubled with that same cough of which I spoke to you when I saw you at Springfield last fall. The convention is making it self contemptible as possible, and seem determined to politically damn themselves in Illinois. You no doubt see full reports of their doings in the papers. In the prison here are some 400 or 500 secesh, and a sorry looking lot they were when they entered the walls. You may think it singular that I should address you, but the “document” is my excuse. If you are acquainted with Mr. Andrews from this place please give him my regards. Yours, &c Thomas S. Pinckard P. S. I found the enclosed among a lot of old manuscripts in a loft in the old Journal office. I have some more of the papers referring to the same affair, but they are only “copies” of originals.

text: Fairfax Court House March 14th 1862. My Dear Sir. The situation of the Army of the Potomac at present is about as follows: Keyes' Division in reserve at Prospect Hill, with a Regiment of Cavalry (Rush) in advance; McCall at Hunter's Mills; Smith at Flint Hill; Porter & Franklin at this place; McDowell in advance towards Centreville; Blenker near the Railroad, in advance of Burlse's Station; Cooke's Cavalry Brigade between Blenker & Fairfax Station; Sumner at Union Mills & Manassas, with one regiment thrown forward to guard Stoneman's forage train, — Gen. Stoneman being en route to the Rappahannock with ten squadrons of Cavalry. The orders of Gen. Stoneman are to capture or drive in any force he may find on this side of the Rappahannock, and to reconnoitre

text: Head Quarters, Baltimore, 15, March 1862. Sir: I have had the honor to receive your kind letter of this morning and hasten to acknowledge it. I will only ask a moment of your attention now to two points. 1. Genl. Banks, Genl. Butler and myself, though named by you as Maj. Genls. on different days were appointed by you, and confirmed by the Senate to take rank from the 16th of May. Banks's name was placed first, mine second, and Butler's third. I raised a question of precedence between Banks and myself under the Army Regulations: it was decided in my favor by Lieut. Genl. Scott on a reference from the War Department; and was very handsomely acquiesced in by Genl. Banks, who said it was proper &

text: May 7th — 1863. Mr President: I have the honor to acknowledge your communication of this date, and in answer have to state that I do not deem it expedient to suspend operations on this line from the reverse we have experienced in endeavoring to extricate the army from its present position. If in the first effort we failed it was not from want of strength or conduct of the small number of the troops actually engaged, but from a cause which could not be foreseen, and could not be provided against. After its occurrence the chances of success were so much lessened, that I felt another plan might be adopted in place of that we were engaged in, which would be more certain in its results: at all events, a failure would not involve disaster, while in the other case it was certain to follow the absence of success— I may add that this consideration almost wholly determined me in ordering the army to return to its old Camp. As to the best time for renewing our advance upon the enemy, I can only decide after an opportunity has been afforded to learn the feeling of the troops— They should not be discouraged or depressed, for

text: Leavenworth, Kan. May 28th 1863. Dear Sir:— As a warm personal friend and supporter of your Administration and war policy, I deem it my duty to apprise you of the dissatisfaction among the loyal people in this Extre state, and elsewhere in the west; as well as among the troops composing the Army of the Frontier; at the appointment of Gen J. M. Schofield to the command of the Dep't of the Missouri, thereby placing Gen Blunt in a subordinate position, to one who has vilified him while victorious and who will not hesitate to pursue when he may have the power to do, through a mistaken policy or kindness. This action causes great exultation among copperheads and rebel sympathizers, and by them is considered a victory. On the other hand your best friends are discouraged by the change. The loyal people and
title: Abraham Lincoln papers: Series 1. General Correspondence. 1833-1916: Mark W. Delahay to Abraham Lincoln, Thursday, May 28, 1863 (Dissatisfaction with appointment of General Schofield)

text: upon him. He is not only willing, but really desires to come back, and he is now at Washington, hoping that some such arrangement may be made. Gen. Hooker told me that he would not only have no objection to, but, circumstances being so, as above described, would desire his return. Would it not be possible to you to make some honorable provision for Gen. Howard, who also declares, that he will not stand in Gen. Sigels way? We have suffered as much insult and disgrace, as human nature can endure. We are also willing to sacrifice ourselves, one and all, and I pray you, let it be, not to atone for blunders, but for some better purpose. It is hardly necessary that I should remind you of the confidential character of this letter. I address myself to you in the anxiety of my heart, you being the father of all of us, and I assure you, that no personal interests of mine are at all connected with this request I

text: Frankfort Ky June 8th 1863 It has been so long since you left here that you can have but little recollection of me, but the importance of the subject upon which I write precludes any apology for this letter, and further I know no one in your City to whom it is more fitting that it should be addressed unless it be to your Father, to whom I wish you to shew it and also ask his aid in accomplishing the object which I seek. The grand son of William S. Waller decd. the old friend and connection of your Father is I learn thro' the papers has been convicted by military authority on some office against the rules or laws of war & is now under sentence of Capital punishment. I know of but little of his case but so far as I can learn it appears to me that the sentence against him is one of more severity than is required to vindicate the rights and security of the Union. May I therefore ask your aid and that of your Father to aid me to obtain from the President, a mitigation of young William S Wallers sentence from Capital punishment to confinement in some military prison during the war,
title: Abraham Lincoln papers: Series 1. General Correspondence. 1833-1916: Harrison Blanton to Montgomery Blair, Monday, June 08, 1863 (Case of William Waller)

text: whole subject and then be intrusted only to some officer of ability and judgment to whom the President would be willing to give the necessary powers. He must have power and the President's confidence. Therefore I do not propose my self for this work. But I make him the following suggestions — it being understood that I am thrown out of the question — namely: Make a Dep't. of the Country west of the Mppi — Louisiana excluded — send them a suitable officer — give him full command of the Dept. & the white troops — Govr Gamble himself included — & let him draw the colored troops togather from every quarter — and organize and consolidate them. He will have the whole line of the Mppi. river for his operations — and draw the Colored men from the free North & the freed men from the entire South. In this way the west country and the Mppi river would be closed to the Confederacy by an Army of 200000 men which at the proper time could take a deciding part in the war. This is my view of the subject, but is this time yet come? Will the President realize that if this summer's campaigns are not

text: McClellan is far our ablest commander. As such he was recommended to You by Genl. Scott after Bull-Run. The Prince de Joinville so regards him; so does the Hungarian officer in the Confederate Service, who wrote the able article in the Cologne Gazette. A military Critic at Berlin spoke of him in that light. Mr Motley writes that he was so regarded at Vienna. Genl. Lee told a British officer, who writes an article in Blackwood, that after Pope's reverses, McClellan restored our shattered forces “as with an enchanter's wand.” You yourself told me, that no battles could have been better fought than South Mountain & Antietam; (& what did not those battles avert of disaster & shame!) & when Burnside was appointed to take his place, he declared that McClellan was the only man capable of Commanding the army.— The Report of the War Committee

text: Your memorialist further states, that he is advised that this proceeding is clearly in violation of the Constitution and laws of the United States, and the Constitution and Laws of Maryland, in utter disregard of the solemn duty of said officers the Provost Marshal and Military Governor enforced by their oaths to execute and obey the Constitution and Laws, destructive of all rights of private property secured to a citizen and a tyranical exercise of arbitrary power — to which he cannot believe your Excellency will suffer to go unrebuked and unredressed Your memorialist further states he is a Loyal Citizen of the United States earnestly and zealously aiding according to his best ability the efforts of the Government to put down the Rebellion now threatening its existence, and has never by word or act given aid or comfort to those in Rebellion against the Government, and he claims to be entitled to the protection of all the laws of the land securing the rights of such citizens to the full enjoyment of their property— Your memorialist forbears to enlarge on the consequences which must inevitably result from such subversion of law, and invasion of private rights, but he submits that if such proceedings as before represented be sanctioned by

text: Philadelphia June 28th 1863 Sir— The large pecuniary interest I represent will be my apology for troubling you with a few remarks upon a subject which I think worthy of your earnest and prompt consideration— It is the extraordinary apathy that pervades the public mind in relation to the Advance of Lees Army into Pennsylvania. This apathy cannot be explained by any want of appreciation of the mortification and sacrifices of honor that must ensue to its citizens, and the desolation that will follow the occupation of the State by the Rebels. These seem to have been duly considered— It is thought however that it arises from a decided impression among the reasoning portion of the masses, that nothing but disaster will attend the movements of the new troops, if they are to go into the field under
title: Abraham Lincoln papers: Series 1. General Correspondence. 1833-1916: John E. Thomson to Abraham Lincoln, Sunday, June 28, 1863 (Lee's invasion of Pennsylvania)

text: confidence in his ability and zeal — but his call for troops will hardly meet with that response which the urgency of the occasion requires— I would therefore suggest as the result of my conviction as to the best interests of the Country, — not the substitution of Genl. McClellan for Genl. Dana, — but that the army in Pennsylvania be placed under the General Command of the former— I am aware of the obstacles to this movement, but in my humble judgement, they should yield to the necessities of the present Emergency. With my best

text: Philadelphia, July 1. 1863 Sir I telegraphed you yesterday urging that Gen McClellan be assigned to duty here as commander of the Dept. & briefly gave the reasons which, in my jugment, demanded such a change. In reply I have your telegram suggesting the difficulties which would attend the restoration of Gen McClellan to active service. I am well aware that some ardent friends of the Administration are resolutely determined that Gen McClellan shall not be called to any office of usefulness — or, if called, they would sacrifice our cause to sacrifice him. This feeling was painfully manifested here yesterday when his call to Penna was decreed possible. That there are others, with unfaltering fidelity to the government, who believe that Gen McC, is not himself faithful, & cannot therefore be useful in any command, is true; and from these classes you have been threatened with the new “leaks” and new “clamors” in case he should be assigned to duty. I am not in any sense a partizan of Gen McC. I do not know him personally; have never communicated with him person directly or indirectly, and probably would not if I had the power, place him at the head of an army to lead offensive operations Nor would I call him to the field if it involved in any
title: Abraham Lincoln papers: Series 1. General Correspondence. 1833-1916: Alexander K. McClure to Abraham Lincoln, Wednesday, July 01, 1863 (Writes in favor of giving McClellan a command in Pennsylvania)

text: degree, the humiliation of the administration. To maintain its dignity & power is of paramount importance, and to impair them is to peril our nationality But, in my judgment, the call of Gen McC to Penna in this crisis would have been attended with the most fortunate results Had it been done when the foe hurled his army upon our border, there would have been a degree of unanimity in his support & a success in organizing troops that would has been measurably if not entirely decisive alike in protecting us, and in relieving the army of the Potomac from the perilous duty of [uncovering?] Washington The period may now be past when the full measure of Gen McC's usefulness can be realized, as delay has invited the fiercest hostility to his call here, — some from honest, and still more from most unworthy motives. Still, I would call him because it is right that he should be here; because he is peculiarly fitted for the task of organizing raw troops & defending our state; because he would be earnestly sustained by thousands of loyal men in the Democratic ranks who are poisoned against the government, & disloyal leaders would be compelled to follow them; and last but not least, because it would clearly charge the Democratic party with its just share of responsibility in defending our State
title: Abraham Lincoln papers: Series 1. General Correspondence. 1833-1916: Alexander K. McClure to Abraham Lincoln, Wednesday, July 01, 1863 (Writes in favor of giving McClellan a command in Pennsylvania)

text: assured that I am your friend, nor can any act of your administration make me anything else, for in your success is [united] the hope, the life of the Republic. I have therefore written with the frankness of a friend, as such at least receive it — & with your better information & judgment decide. Gen Couch has done his whole duty. In head, in heart & in effort he has performed the cruel task assigned him as far as mortal could; but he cannot make or unmake sentiment, & the State has seemed lifeless even with the foe at our doors & in our homes. I go to Harrisburg to-day Truly Thine A K McClure
title: Abraham Lincoln papers: Series 1. General Correspondence. 1833-1916: Alexander K. McClure to Abraham Lincoln, Wednesday, July 01, 1863 (Writes in favor of giving McClellan a command in Pennsylvania)

text: Louisiana Mo. July 6th 1863 Dear Sir— Through a friend I learn have just learned that a movement is on foot among some pestiferous politicians to bring about a change of commanders in this Department, in other words to secure the reappointment of Genl Curtis. We are now in comparative peace in Missouri. The people have confidence in Genl Schofield and feeling assured of the good intentions of the administration toward them no considerable uprising can be brought about. Nine tenths of the people every-where in the State are disposed to acquiesce in the recent ordinance of the Convention, abolishing slavery prospectively. The elements opposing it among the people, are the same that opposed it in the convention, — the radical revolutionists, and the original secessionists. The ordinance is not exactly as I would have had it, but it is better than I expected, and secures all
title: Abraham Lincoln papers: Series 1. General Correspondence. 1833-1916: John B. Henderson to Abraham Lincoln, Monday, July 06, 1863 (Military affairs in Missouri)

text: Te Deum Laudamus! New-York 6 July 1863 Anniversary of Thermopylae My dear Sumner, I write to You very much because I have no one else to say it to — and I write, very much because I cannot help uttering it — that now is the time, now is the time that Government should briskly proceed with the Concription; for the two reasons that we want now troops more than ever, and that the draft would now proceed easier.
title: Abraham Lincoln papers: Series 1. General Correspondence. 1833-1916: Francis Lieber to Charles Sumner, Monday, July 06, 1863 (Recommends government begin conscription)

text: Now is the time. What I said on page 9 of my address is most assuredly well founded. I send a copy and mark the passage. The Rebellion can never be stopped, unless it be crushed, and it cannot be crushed, unless we have a gigantic army that can both, annihilate on points, and run out in different directions without being materially weakend. If I ever saw anything dear I see this. I speak for many. Is there no way of pushing this draft vigorously? Of course we cannot do anything
title: Abraham Lincoln papers: Series 1. General Correspondence. 1833-1916: Francis Lieber to Charles Sumner, Monday, July 06, 1863 (Recommends government begin conscription)

text: Vol. Cavalry, Grand Rapids, July 10th 1863 Sir In behalf of thousands of my Constituents I congratulate you upon the success which has attended our arms and the brilliant victories we have won in Pensylvania and the South West The capture of Vicksburg and the defeat of Gen'l Lee have filled the whole Country with rejoicings — inspired the People with fresh courage and increased their faith and confidence in your Administration We feel that we have something tangible on which to rest our belief that the Rebellion will be put down and our glorious Union preserved & perpetuated for our
title: Abraham Lincoln papers: Series 1. General Correspondence. 1833-1916: Francis W. Kellogg to Abraham Lincoln, Friday, July 10, 1863 (Congratulations for the recent victories)

text: posterity There is but one feeling now among loyal & patriotic men in this part of the Country and I cannot doubt that it is universal We want the war prosecuted with such vigor that the rebel armies shall have no opportunity to recover from their defeat To that end we hope and pray that you will order a Draft for 400 or 500,000 men that the Nation may feel assured of the speedy suppression of the rebellion — the rebel leaders and armies be disheartened and the brave men who survive the bloody battles of the last week be encouraged by the knowledge that the ranks of thin & battered regiments will soon be filled and their numbers render victory easy & certain hereafter Again I congratulate your Excellency and pray God to inspire you and your Counsellors with wisdom and bless your efforts in the Future as He has done in the Past till Peace shall smile upon our Land and a united People shall again be happy and prosperous under the protecting aegis of our glorious Constitution With the highest respect I have the honor to be Your Ob't Serv't F W Kellogg MC 4th Dis't Michigan
title: Abraham Lincoln papers: Series 1. General Correspondence. 1833-1916: Francis W. Kellogg to Abraham Lincoln, Friday, July 10, 1863 (Congratulations for the recent victories)

text: that all our efforts to obtain permission to send a Surgeon to him, had utterly failed, I decided to go & see for myself, so on Saturday I left for Gettysburg & reached there on Tuesday, after having crossed the Susquehanna in a skiff, & ridden twenty three miles in a Cattle pen— Every thing in Gettysburg is in the utmost confusion — no provisions of any kind can be obtained, & the atmosphere of the whole town is absolutely stifling— We spent the entire morning in visiting the numerous hospitals in, & around the town, in search of Robert, & at last ascertained that he had been removed to the College, where we found him in a most deplorable condition — his hand is broken, & he is wounded in the ancle by a shell — & seems much weakened by all he has gone through, & his present privations — he has neither pillow, nor bed, & sleeps on a quilt spread upon the floor— There are about six hundred Confederates in this Hospital, the greater portion of whom are desperately wounded, & from the scarcity of nurses, — I saw but two — & the want of every kind of attention, they suffer Terribly — the pestilential air of the whole building, is of itself alone, enough to kill them If it is quite impossible for us to bring Robert home, dont you think we might get him transferred to a Hospital in this City, where we could give him the care he so sorely needs— With many thanks for the kind interest manifested in his behalf, by yourself & family. I remain yours most affectionately Mary. L. Fendall
title: Abraham Lincoln papers: Series 1. General Correspondence. 1833-1916: Mary L. Fendall to Mrs. Stephen P. Lee, Saturday, July 18, 1863 (Account of visit to Gettysburg to find a wounded relative)

text: you by me, in which the people of the State of Kansas, naturally feel a deep interest in, because the State of Kansas has never yet been treated as other loyal States are treated. You will remember that I asked that Kansas, be placed under one Military Commander instead of two, as is now the case. Maj Genl. Blunt having the Command of the southern & Brig Genl Ewing the northern portion of the State. I gave you my reasons fully in my communications to you under date of 5th & 25 June last why I wished Maj Genl Blunt's military authority to be absolutely suspended in the State of Kansas. I also asked that all orders from the War Department, that Maj Genl. Blunt Shall name the officers for me as the Govr of Kansas to Commission be revoked. I asked that Lt Col. J. M. Williams Commissioned by the Secretary of War, be dismissed the Service, and that R. C. Anderson Commissioned by me on the 20th of Feby 1863, be made Col. of the 1st Kansas Colored Regiment. My reasons for this change you will find fully set forth in my previous Communications to you upon this subject. When I refused to commission Capt J. M. Williams Lt. Col. then in the attitude of defying the Civil authorities (two indictments then being pending against him) every paper in the State sustained me, and when the Secretary of War, done what I refused to do, and by so doing foisted upon the State an outlaw in high military position, almost every paper in the State, denounced him for thus interfering with the rights they naturally expected to be exercised by the Chief Executive of the State, which usage Custom & law had given to all the States. Some time last Apl, the Hon. Secretary of War, when asked to dismiss Lt Col. J. M. Williams the service, informed me orrally that the Case would be refered to Maj Genl. Curtis St Louis, then Military Commandant of the Department of the Missouri for examination & decission. On enquiry at that Department, I was informed no such papers from the Secretary of War upon that Subject had been received. Please inform me your decision upon all the subjects mentioned at your earliest Convenience addressed to me at Topeka Kansas, where I am now on my way. I very much regret thus to be compelled to trouble you, but duty to myself & duty to my State leaves me no alternative. I am with much respect Your Obt. Servt Thos Carney Gov of Kansas.

text: blackened in the Press not only of this country but of Europe also, for an occurrence for which I least of all was responsible — and to suffer this without being permitted to defend myself. I had to submit to the mortification of seeing my rights of seniority disregarded, first in the case of Gen. Newton, my junior, who was placed in command of the 1st Corps, and then in that of Gen. Hayes, a Brigadier, who now commands the 2d Corps — while I had had to give up the command of the 11th Corps to Gen Howard on account of his seniority. I waived my claims, leaving all, without murmur, to the judgment of the General comanding the army, whom I did not want to embarrass in the midst of a campaign. I asked him only to give me such reinforcements, as would render my command respectable, efficient and to a certain extent corresponding with my rank. Gen. Meade replied that my request was modest and just and that he would do so at the earliest opportunity. That was before we recrossed the Potomac, and I have not received a single man, and my command remains a merely nominal one, hardly men enough to make up respectable Brigade. If there had been any complaint about me, I would say nothing. But nobody ever dared to assert, that I did not do my duty to the best satisfaction of my superior officers. I do not see why I should have had to submit to such treatment in this army, save for the reason that I am a “foreigner” and an antislavery-man. Such things can be borne as long as there is a reasonable prospect of improvement. But if there be none — and judging from present appearances I do not
title: Abraham Lincoln papers: Series 1. General Correspondence. 1833-1916: Carl Schurz to Abraham Lincoln, Saturday, August 08, 1863 (Breaking up of 11th Corps)

text: see any — it would be a useless sacrifice of self respect if I remained where I do not seem to be wanted. If Gen. Meade would carry out his original plan to reorganize the Army in four Corps of two divisions each, it would be possible for me to stay, as this would place me approximately upon a level with other officers. But this matter seems to be indefinitely postponed. Your wise and well meaning plan to let the 11th Corps remain in existence until Gen. Meade, Gen. Howard and myself could agree upon some other expedient is also set aside by the breaking up of the Corps without our consent; for to call the two small remaining divisions an “Army-Corps” would be ridiculous.— Things being in that state, could you not save me from the necessity of resigning by assigning me together with my small command to some other duty? As Gen. Halleck is opposed to the occupation of the Shenandoah-Valley, that plan, I expect, has to be dropped. But would it not be possible to give me the Department of Western Virginia, which is now, — I suppose only temporarily — in the hands of a Brigadier? I would then concentrate some troops in the Kanawha Valley and orgainize expeditions with a view to the destruction of the Lynchburg railroad, a thing which ought to have been done long ago. If my division, comprising only about 2400 muskets, is withdrawn from this Army, it might easily be replaced by troops from Harpers Ferry, those,

This would appear tempting to me also, were it not that in view of recent events in Mexico, I am greatly impressed with the importance of re-establishing the national authority in Western Texas, as soon as possible— I am not making an order, however— That I leave, for the present at least, to the General-in-Chief— A word upon another subject. Now, I think at least a hundred thousand can, and ought to be rapidly organized along the river it's shores, relieving all white troops to serve elsewhere. text: Rosecrans are all engaged now in an effort to relieve your section. But remember, you will probably thwart them if you make this public. [Copy in John Hay's hand:] Executive Mansion, Washington, August 9, 1863. Gentlemen: The petition of which you were the bearers, has just been handed me. Your cards and notes had come to me on two or three successive days before, and I knew then, as well as I do now, after reading the petition, what your mission was. I knew it was the same true and painful story, which Gov. Johnson, Mr. Maynard, Dr. Clements and others have been telling me for more than two years. I also knew that meeting you could do no good; because I have all the while done, and shall continue to do the best for you I could, and can. I do as much for East Tennessee as I would or could, if my own home, and family were in Knoxville. The difficulties of getting a Union army into that region, and of keeping it there, are so apparent, so obvious, that none can fail to see them, unless it may be those who are driven mad and blind by their sufferings. Start by whatever route they may, their lines of supply are broken before they get half- way. A small force sufficient to beat the enemy now there, would be of no value, because the enemy would re-inforce to meet them, until we should have to give back, or accumulate so large a force, as to be very difficult to supply, and as to ruin us entirely if a great disaster should befal it. I know you are too much distressed to be argued with, and therefore I do not attempt it at length. You know I am not indifferent to your troubles; else I should not, more than a year and a half ago, have made the effort I did to have a Rail Road built on purpose to relieve you. The Secretary of War, Gen. Halleck, Gen. Burnside and Gen. Rosecrans are all engaged now in an effort to relieve your section. But remember, you will probably thwart them, if you make this public.

Dear Sir:— Being at Cincinnatti last night, I met the Missouri Delegation (some 70) who will be in Washington by the time you get this to ask of the President, among other things, the displacement of Gen. Schofield. I will not ask for it, but would like to be there, should a change be made. My former business in that State, and my knowledge of its people and of their present troubles would be of service to me, and many considerations induce the confidence, that such an assignment would be acceptable there. You may not

text: free negroes. Visiting this City and protected by the assumed authority of Mr Commissioner Cox, these desparadoes break into the houses of colored citizens, thrust loaded pistols into the faces of terrified women and screaming children, and then, protected by legal papers bear off their victims to the tender mercies of the lash and prison, or the hopeless martyrdom of Southern slavery. Along the borders of the Potomac below this City male slaves are now being mustered in gangs and sent over to Virginia as contributions by their Masters to the cause of rebellion, if these men make an effort to escape they are pursued and shot to death by their merciless owners. There is now in Marlborough Jail a negro man whose eyes have been utterly destroyed by a charge of shot fired into his face, and not long since two colored girls were found chained in the garret of a private house in the neighborhood of this City, who after having been cruelly beaten by three men, one of them using a trace chain to inflict the blows, were left, with their backs one mass of festering wounds to the farther horrors of chains and darkness. An instance has just come to my knowledge where a negro woman and three daughters owned by a citizen of this City, still resident here, were sent to Baltimore a few days before the late Emancipation Act was passed, for the sole purpose of evading its provisions, one of those daughters, an intelligent woman, has succeeded in returning to this City and is now claimed as a Slave and threatened with seizure through the agency of Mr Commissioner Cox's summary and illegal writs, It cannot be that such atrocities will be longer permitted, and that men whose every sympathy is with slavery and its co-agent Treason, shall be suffered longer to visit upon the poor slave the hatred they feel for Freedom and the Union. I respectfully ask for such instructions as shall enable me to officially protect the now helpless victims of the Slave owners vengeance, and the perjured oaths of their friends, official and other-wise, in this City and District. I am Sir. Your Obedient Servant. L. C. Baker Col & Provost Marshal War Department.

Mrs. Maltby will represent to Your Excellency the difficulties I labour under in the discharge of my official duties as Collector of Internal Revinue. My District is large— Some four hundred miles in leangth a large portion sparsely populated. My Commissions for the year, will not exceed five thousand dollars, out of this amount, I am required to pay Seven Deputies and all the expences of office rent, office furnature Safes — &c. The Assessor of my district, will receive for his services upwards of three thousand Dollars, for his services, aside from the pay of his Deputies, he is also allowed five hundred dollars per year for office rent, and pay for clerk hire— he has no responsibilities or bonds to give. mine are heavy— I trust that Congress will grant the Collectors out-side of San Francisco some relief. It is true that the State is in a bad condition, and it is equally true that this condition is brought about by professed Union men — radicals. There has been no time, since the beginning of the war when there was so few armed rebels or guerrillas in Missouri as at the present time. The only trouble at all worthy of mention, in comparison with what the state has suffered heretofore, is the lawless acts of radicals in their effort to exterminate, or drive out, all who differ from them in political sentiment. This lawlessness is instigated, encouraged and applauded by the radical press and leaders. Every effort to put down this lawlessness is denounced by the radicals as persecution

Many of The leaders of the present charcoal faction who now war upon General Schofield are not the men who sustained the Government at the beginning of the war. The men who now support Genl Schofield are the identical ones who stood around Lyon, and sustained the Government in the dark days of 1861. They are the true friends of the Government. Men who stand between the rebels on the one hand, and the radical revolutionists on the other — the men who maintain the Constitution, uphold the laws, and advocate justice to all men.
